newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar sheds over 100 points vs mark by Tokyo noon.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sheds over 100 points vs mark by Tokyo noon.

text.p: The dollar lost over 100 points against the mark by midday on Monday due to selling by traders wishing to cut their losses on long positions built recently.

The mark was bought back strongly on renewed pessimism over European economic and monetary union due to possible French general elections, and Italy's proposed mini-budget which has been harshly criticised by the International Monetary Fund.
Dollar selling gained momentum after the greenback easily broke through stop-loss points at 1.7080 and 1.7050 marks, traders said.

"Optimism over EMU receded again due to (possible) French elections and Italy's proposed mini-budget, motivating traders to lighten their long dollar positions against the mark," said a long-term bank trader.

Election fever gripped France on Sunday as speculation mounted President Jacques Chirac would announce a snap election on Monday. Polls showed voters would approve of bringing forward the vote due next March and predicted a close battle.
Chirac's office remained tight-lipped except to deny a report in the daily Le Monde that the president was planning a sharp shift towards free-market economic policies.
Meanwhile, the IMF criticised the Italian government's proposed mini-budget for lacking structural reform measures, the Italian news agency ANSA reported from Washington.
After these series of events over the weekend, traders realised there were risks in holding too many short-mark, long-dollar positions and began to unwind them, traders said.
The dollar's sharp decline against the mark also pushed the greenback down against the yen, traders said.

Earlier, the mark rose against yen on speculative buying in line with Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's remark on Thursday that the mark's level correctly reflected economic fundamentals and that the Bundesbank did not want a weak mark and continued to be interested in having a strong mark.

Elsewhere, Japanese institutional investors sold dollars at around 125.70 yen. The Australian dollar remained weak due to fears that local rates may ease again, which would further narrow Australia's interest rate gap with such countries like Japan, suggesting slowing capital flows from Tokyo to Sydney.
